title: Mixing preserves the fiber and Alice’s bit
statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer, let $p$ be a deterministic protocol for set disjointness on $n$ coordinates, let $z$ be an achievable value of $Z$, and let $\omega_{\mathrm{pair}},\omega$ be hard samples. Suppose $\omega_{\mathrm{pair}}$ lies in the fiber of $Z=z$ and its special-coordinate bit pair is $b=(b_1,b_2)$, while $\omega$ also lies in the fiber of $Z=z$. Then mixing Alice’s input from $\omega_{\mathrm{pair}}$ with Bob’s input from $\omega$ produces a sample in the fiber of $Z=z$ whose Alice special-coordinate bit is $b_1$.
hypotheses_covered: $p$ is a deterministic protocol for set disjointness on $n$ coordinates
The special-coordinate bit pair of $\omega_{\mathrm{pair}}$ is $b$
replaced:
Fix a deterministic disjointness protocol $p$ on inputs of length $n$, and let $z$ be an
achievable value of the variable $Z = (M, T, X_{<T}, Y_{>T})$, whose fiber $Z^{-1}(z)$
is the set of hard-distribution samples mapping to $z$. Let $\omega_{\mathrm{pair}}$ and
$\omega$ be two samples of this fiber, and suppose that the pair of bits at the special
coordinate of $\omega_{\mathrm{pair}}$, namely Alice's bit and Bob's bit there, equals
$b = (b_1, b_2)$. Form the mixed sample by taking Alice's input from
$\omega_{\mathrm{pair}}$ and Bob's input from $\omega$ (keeping their common special
coordinate $T$, the bits of $X$ before $T$, and the bits of $Y$ after $T$). Then this
mixed sample again lies in $Z^{-1}(z)$, and Alice's bit at its special coordinate equals
$b_1$.
